blocks.text: דואר: in Rabba Schemoth fol. 133b, alongside the בן הפילים (skink) and the צב (toad), דואר is also mentioned, which is said to be a kind of toad; but there is still obscurity on this point, and the word still requires further investigation.

המיסו: in Rabba (Bereschit fol. 92b) and the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachoth fol. 12b) it is asked: What are the יומים (Gen. 36, 24)? One said: they are המיונום, i.e. Ἡμιόνοι [hēmionoi], mules; another said: they are המיסו, i.e. ἥμισυ [hēmisy], half-animals, which are half horse, half ass.

Aristotel. (Thiergesch. 6, 29, 4) also mentions two kinds of half-asses, one of which reproduces among its own kind, while the other is sterile (see §. 168), and these two kinds are meant here; המיסו is the kind that was first described again by Pallas in the „Neue Schriften der Petersburger Akademie“ vol. 19, p. 394 as Equus hemionos.
Cf. Frankel: Monatsschrift etc. vol. 3, p. 386.
זביוין, probably for זביבין, see §. 420, note.

חורנם (Jerusalem Talmud A. Sara C. 2, H. 9) may be bought from the heathens and eaten, which is explained as a kind of small salted fish; likewise the מרטיסה mentioned there is said to be a kind of small salted locust.

חיוא דטור, snake of the mountain; in the Jerusalem Talmud C. 8, H. 7 it is said: Someone was preparing melted fat (חום שחיק, §. 92), when a snake of the mountain came and ate of it; now when the house snakes likewise came along to eat of it, the former began a fight with them, pelted them with earth, and finally threw itself into the fat in order to cover and protect it.

חלון; in the Jerusalem Talmud Sabbat C. 1. fol. 3b it is said of the locust חלון that it has neither veins nor bones; with [p. 371] this word Jonathan (as Aruch read) translates the Hebrew צלצל, which denotes the whirring locust (§. 387).
אבחטם, see חמר סלק

חפיתא. According to the Jerusalem Talmud A. Sara C. 2, H. 9, one placed the fish חפיתא in a container (קליפתה) and observed whether it secreted slime, in which case it may be eaten; the word is probably identical with חיפושא (§. 345).
חרדון (Rabba Bereschit fol. 92, c). The toad
חרדון
mates with the snake
חכינא
and brings forth the water snake
חברבר
; cf. on this §. 300.
טפוא (Rabba Bereschit fol. 15a) is the same as שפן (§. 142).

ירודאתא. On the biblical passage (Echa 4, 3): Even the תנין give the breast to their young, the Midrash (Rabba Echa fol. 78. c) adds by way of explanation: These are the ירודאתא, which veil their face with a kind of covering, so that they do not see their young red while suckling and devour them.
The author of Matnat Kehuna explains the word as a kind of snake, which is wrong for the very reason that snakes do not suckle their young.

It seems that the Midrash was thinking of the marsupial, and that addition is to be referred not to the mothers but to the young. As is well known, the young of marsupials, when they are born, are still quite undeveloped and look almost like a naked little lump of flesh; the mother then puts them into the pouch, closes it tight, and now lets the young suck until they are fully developed. For the teats are located inside the pouch.

If we add the words of Rashi on our biblical passage (which agree with Midr. Tanchuma on Bechukotai), our explanation is supported still more; they read: Although the תנין is cruel, it nevertheless bares its breast when it sees its young coming along hungry; it bares the teat from its container, for it has a pouch over the breasts, and it stretches the teats out so that the young one does not shrink back from the pouch.

What is true and what is invented in that explanation is easy to recognize; the marsupials are cruel predators, and a single one strangles 10—20 chickens and ducks at once in order to be able to drink fresh blood (Voigt, l. c. 1. p. 446); these animals are now at home only in America and some in New Holland, but formerly were also present in Europe (ibid. p. 345), and their cruelty [p. 372] may have earned them the name תנין and accordingly ירוראא; both names serve to designate cruel and monstrous animals (see §. 299).

ירודות. In the Jerusalem Talmud Kilajim C. 8. H. 5 it is said that the ירודות and the ostriches (נעמית) are to be regarded as birds in all ritual respects. If we compare with this the Chaldean translation of תנים ובנות יענה (Jes. 43, 20) by ירודין ובנת נעמין, then evidently our ירודות and תנים are identical. We have also seen in §. 299 how Rashi explains תנין as a bird that constantly groans and wails, and the pairing with the ostrich strengthens us in the conjecture expressed there, that by יארוד the eagle species Perknopterus is to be understood. Aristotle (Thierg. 9, 22, 2) describes it thus: This bird has a white head and is the largest of all eagle species, has short wings and a long tail; it resembles the vulture and also bears the name Ὀρειπελαργός [oreipelargos] (mountain stork) and Γυπαιετός [gypaietos] (vulture-eagle), lives in groves and has all the bad qualities of those, but

none of their good ones; for ravens and other birds catch and pursue it. For it is sluggish, and therefore does not know how to feed itself well, carries carrion about with it, and cries and wails when it is hungry.
The quality of its size and the shortness of its wings explain its pairing with the ostrich, and the aforementioned wailing is, as mentioned, also noted by Rashi.
סיליי see כילוי.
ארי נמירון see כלב אגריון.

כלך, which we explained above (§. 509) as floss silk, is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Sabbat C. 2. fol. 4, c) by יאנבון קיסריי: Ascheri on Kilajim 9, 2 has אצבין קסרי and explains it as a kind of wool that is found growing on stones in the Mediterranean Sea.
